title: Passing Arguments by Value, Pointer, and Reference
relevance: Interviewers use swap-style examples to check whether a candidate understands when a function can modify the caller's variables versus working only on copies.

phases.goal: Establish the three argument-passing mechanisms and what each parameter actually is.

must_hit.point: By default, arguments are passed by value: the function receives copies of the caller's data in its own parameters.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says parameters are copies of the caller's values, not the originals themselves.

must_hit.point: Call by pointer passes addresses so the function can operate on the caller's variables through dereferencing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions passing &x/&y (or addresses) and using *a/*b to reach the originals.

must_hit.point: Call by reference makes parameters aliases for the caller's variables—same objects under new names, not copies and not addresses to dereference.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes reference parameters as aliases sharing the caller's storage.

probes: What are the three ways a C++ function can receive arguments, and what does each parameter actually represent?

hints.1: Think about whether the function gets a copy, an address, or another name for the same object.
hints.2: Map each mechanism to: by value → copies; by pointer → addresses you dereference; by reference → aliases.
hints.3: Default is by value (copies). Pointers hold addresses and use * to modify originals. References are aliases for the caller's variables.

phases.goal: Show how each mechanism behaves in a swap and what happens to the caller's x and y.

must_hit.point: In call-by-value swap, a and b are exchanged inside the function's activation record, but the caller's x and y stay unchanged (still 10 20).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains that only the copies swap and vanish on return, so cout prints 10 20.

must_hit.point: In call-by-pointer swap, a and b hold addresses of x and y; *a and *b write through to main's memory so the values become 20 10.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes swap(&x, &y), dereferencing pointers, and the swapped output 20 10.

must_hit.point: In call-by-reference swap, call syntax is swap(x, y) like by value, but because a and b are x and y, the exchange updates the originals to 20 10.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes ordinary call syntax with reference parameters that are the same objects as x and y.

must_hit.point: With references, no copies are made: reference parameters share main's storage (x/a and y/b name the same cells).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says x and a (and y and b) refer to the same storage rather than duplicated values.

probes: Walk through swap by value, by pointer, and by reference: what happens to x and y in main after each call?

hints.1: Start with by-value swap and ask whether main's variables can change.
hints.2: Contrast: by value swaps copies; by pointer swaps via *a/*b; by reference swaps because a/b are aliases.
hints.3: By value → still 10 20. By pointer with &x,&y and *a,*b → 20 10. By reference with swap(x,y) → 20 10 because a/b are x/y.

phases.goal: Separate argument-passing semantics from inlining, and state the space-versus-speed cost of inlining.

must_hit.point: Inlining is a compiler optimisation about how a call is executed, independent of how arguments are passed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly separates pass-by-reference/value/pointer from whether the call is inlined.

must_hit.point: Not inlined: the function body exists once (smaller executable) but each call pays for a jump and a return; inlined: code runs in place with no jump (faster) but the body is duplicated at every call site, enlarging the executable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the space-for-speed trade: one copy plus jump/return versus duplicated bodies and no jump.

must_hit.point: In modern C++ the inline keyword is only a suggestion; compilers such as GCC, Clang, and MSVC decide whether inlining is worthwhile by weighing speed gain against code-size cost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says inline does not force inlining; the compiler chooses based on speed vs size.

probes: If a call-by-reference function is also marked inline, what does inlining change—and what does it not change?

hints.1: Inlining is about call execution, not about copies versus aliases.
hints.2: Compare one shared body with jump/return versus pasting the body at each call site.
hints.3: Inlining removes jump-and-return and may enlarge the binary; it does not change whether parameters are values, pointers, or references. inline is only a suggestion.

phases.goal: Identify why reference parameters are the idiomatic C++ choice when a function should modify the caller.

must_hit.point: Reference parameters unite the clean call syntax of value passing with the power to modify the caller's data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says you call swap(x, y) like by value, yet the originals are modified.

must_hit.point: Because of that combination of syntax and mutability, reference parameters are the idiomatic C++ choice for this role.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States references as the preferred/idiomatic mechanism when the callee should change caller state.

probes: When you want a function to modify the caller's variables, why prefer pass-by-reference over pass-by-value or pass-by-pointer in idiomatic C++?

hints.1: Compare call-site appearance and whether the originals can change.
hints.2: By value looks clean but cannot modify; by pointer can modify but needs & and *; references do both.
hints.3: Use int& aliases: same swap(x,y) syntax as by value, no copies, modifies caller—hence the idiomatic C++ choice.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Normal calls keep one copy of the machine code and pay jump-and-return at each site; inlining pastes the body into each call site for speed with no jump, but duplicates code and enlarges the executable. Argument-passing mode is independent of that choice.

tradeoffs.topic: Pass by value vs pass by reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: By value uses clean call syntax but only copies, so caller variables cannot change; by reference keeps that same call syntax while making parameters aliases that share the caller's storage and can modify originals.

tradeoffs.topic: Pass by pointer vs pass by reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both can modify the caller: pointers take addresses and require dereferencing; references are aliases with ordinary call syntax and are the idiomatic C++ choice for that power plus clean syntax.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a by-value swap changes the caller's variables because the parameters were swapped inside the function.
gotchas.correction: Only the copies in the callee's activation record are exchanged; they vanish on return, so the caller's x and y remain 10 20.

gotchas.trap: Treating identical call syntax swap(x, y) as proof that by-value and by-reference behave the same.
gotchas.correction: The call looks the same, but reference parameters are aliases for x and y, so the exchange updates the originals to 20 10.

gotchas.trap: Thinking the inline keyword guarantees the function body is inlined.
gotchas.correction: In modern C++, inline is only a suggestion; compilers decide whether inlining is worthwhile by weighing speed against code size.
